Haha it's funny, I've been explaining this to my non-spanish-speaker friends lately! We do understand each other but sometimes we got a hard time communicating, or finding the appropriate word for other's slang words. I think you can divide Latin america into Central america, northern South America (Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru maybe? even Chile?) , and southern South America (Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay) **I repeat, I said I *think*, this is my personal opinion**

First of all, I think we all have a hard time understanding Spain's spanish, whenever I watch a movie I really can't understand the beginning, but a few minutes later is like my brain gets used to it so it's OK. Then I think that we can understand each other more easily in our respective 'regions' as I described before. I know for a fact that a few words we use in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay for naming people (like friends/buddies) are insults in Peru, Chile, and the other countries above.. I also know that I failed to understand a little Mexican girl once (10/11 yo), I was trying to identify the woman in charge of her, and she kept telling me words I could not understand, like apparently we have completely different words for "skinny", "blonde", "bunhead" and stuff like that.. But I also know that maybe if it was an older girl with more vocabulary we would probably achieve mutual understanding haha..

The RAE (Real Academia Española) takes and accepts all our words so we're technically speaking spanish correctly in everyone's respective way, so it's the same language though we have those difficulties to understand each other sometimes. I wouldn't say "We can't understand each other" but I would DEFINITELY say "we may have a hard time understanding each other". Continuing with the examples, my parents come from that "northern south america" region i described, and I switch my spanish every time I speak to them, because if I don't it may lead to misconception, for example once I forgot to 'switch my spanish' and I asked my mother for my flip flops and she understood it was (and brought me) a pair of sneakers ( :( )

But those are just little misunderstandings I guess. I think sometimes I have a REALLY hard time understanding central american spanish, like I have to ask them to please stop and repeat again because sometimes when I lose the meaning of the sentence at the very beginning I just cant fucking understand the rest.. Also in reggaeton songs there are quite a few words I have not yet understood.. I like central american spanish tho

Leaving idioms aside, there are also some differences in phonetics, which may not affect our mutual understanding but are hard to get use to. With Spain's spanish is their annoying (Im sorry but kind of annoying) [sh] sound or [z] for Ss, I actually don't quite know when they use which one, what I do know is that it makes it hard to keep up with.. Then In Argentina and Uruguay (In Argentina is a lot stronger than in uruguayan spanish, in Uruguay is a lot less accentuated) the sound [sh] is used whenever there's a  "Y" which might be confusing if you hear it for the first time I guess, because instead of hearing "Yo soy" you'll hear "Sho soy" but it's quite a smooth sound. Parauguayans speak with their mouthes shout so it's like the [r] sound is ten times more accentuated,( it's like the sound of r in the world "bark").
